questions.question: Why can anyone write and run tests without a testing framework?
options: Because tests are not code
A test just calls your function with known inputs and checks the result; a framework is a convenience, not a requirement
Because JavaScript and Python include a built-in test generator
Because tests only work if you install Mocha or unittest first
questions.explanation: A test is just code that calls your function and compares the actual output to the expected output. Frameworks add organization and nicer reporting, but the core idea needs nothing special.

questions.question: What does a unit test check?
options: That one small piece of code (e.g., a single function) returns the expected result for given inputs
That all imports are alphabetized
That the whole application works end to end in production
That the code is formatted consistently
questions.explanation: Unit tests exercise small, isolated pieces of code. Formatting and import order are checked by other tools (formatters, import sorters).

questions.question: Which is the best reason to test `rps("x", "x")` even though a tie test already exists?
options: Because "x" is a valid hand
Because tests must always be run in pairs
It is an edge case: two identical but invalid hands should return "Invalid", not "Tie!"
Because Mocha requires at least two identical arguments
questions.explanation: Good tests probe boundaries and edge cases. A function can pass every happy-path test yet still return "Tie!" for two equal invalid values.

questions.question: What is a code formatter (e.g., Prettier, Black) responsible for?
options: Installing dependencies
Finding logic bugs such as unreachable code
Automatically rewriting code to follow consistent style (indentation, line width, quotes, spacing)
Running the test suite
questions.explanation: Formatters change how code looks, not what it does. This keeps a team's code uniform and avoids style arguments in code review.

questions.question: What is a linter (e.g., ESLint, flake8) mainly used for?
options: Running tests and reporting coverage
Compiling code to machine language
Rewriting all code into one consistent layout automatically
Statically analyzing code for likely errors, style violations, and bad practices (like unused variables), usually without changing behavior
questions.explanation: Linters examine code without running it and point out potential problems. They may auto-fix a few things, but many findings must be fixed by hand.

questions.question: Which statement best describes the difference between a formatter and a linter?
options: They do exactly the same thing
A formatter runs your tests; a linter installs packages
A formatter finds bugs; a linter fixes whitespace
A formatter standardizes how code looks; a linter flags potential errors and questionable patterns
questions.explanation: Formatters normalize layout. Linters analyze code quality (unused imports, undefined names, suspicious constructs). Teams typically use both.

questions.question: Why do the lab's instructions create a `.flake8` file with `max-line-length = 88`?
options: Because Python cannot run lines longer than 88 characters
To make isort sort imports faster
So flake8's rules match Black's formatting (Black wraps at 88 characters, while flake8 defaults to 79)
To tell Black which files to ignore
questions.explanation: Without matching settings, a file Black formatted could still be flagged by flake8 for line length. Aligning the two avoids contradictory tool output.

questions.question: What does `isort` do, and why do some teams run it?
options: It checks that imports work at runtime
It installs missing packages from PyPI
It removes unused imports and deletes unused files
It sorts and groups Python import statements into a consistent order, keeping imports tidy and diffs small
questions.explanation: isort only reorders (and groups) imports. Consistent ordering makes files easier to read and reduces merge noise. It doesn't judge whether an import is used.

questions.question: In `package.json`, why are `mocha`, `prettier`, and `eslint` installed with `--save-dev`?
options: Because they cannot be installed any other way
They are tools needed while developing (testing, formatting, linting), not required for the app to run
Because they must be committed to GitHub inside `node_modules`
Because `--save-dev` makes them install faster
questions.explanation: devDependencies are tools for development and CI. Runtime libraries go under `dependencies`.

questions.question: What is the benefit of defining scripts like `"lint:check"` and `"format:fix"` in `package.json`?
options: They prevent Prettier and ESLint from conflicting
Everyone can run the same commands with `npm run <name>`, so the team uses identical tool settings
They make the tools run automatically on every save
They install the tools globally
questions.explanation: Scripts give the team shared, named commands. They don't run automatically, but they make the checks easy to repeat locally and in CI.

questions.question: Black and Prettier both reformat files. What does it mean that running the formatter a second time should change nothing?
options: Formatting is idempotent: once code follows the style, the tool finds nothing to fix
The tool only works once per project
The code has no tests
The formatter failed silently
questions.explanation: A formatter converges on one canonical layout. If a second run still changes files, something is wrong or a different tool/version is in play.

questions.question: A team's CI pipeline runs the test suite, formatter check, linter, and import sorter on every pull request. What is the main benefit?
options: Problems are caught automatically before code is merged, keeping the main branch consistent and maintainable
It guarantees the code has no bugs
It removes the need to write tests
It replaces the need for code review
questions.explanation: Automated checks catch regressions and style issues early and consistently. They don't guarantee correctness or replace human review.

questions.question: Which command checks Python formatting with Black WITHOUT changing any files?
options: `poetry run isort .`
`poetry run flake8 --fix .`
`poetry run black --check .`
`poetry run black .`
questions.explanation: `--check` reports which files would change but leaves them alone. Plain `black .` rewrites files, and flake8 has no `--fix` option.

questions.question: Which JavaScript command lists style violations with Prettier WITHOUT rewriting files?
options: `npm run format:fix`
`npm run format:check`
`npm test`
`npm run lint:fix`
questions.explanation: `format:check` runs `prettier --check`; `format:fix` runs `prettier --write` and changes your files. `lint:fix` is ESLint's auto-fix.
